synopsis: The booklet recommends reference class forecasting plus schedule-risk analysis as the primary schedule approach, but the outside view is credible only with genuinely similar historical work; the cited 2016 comparison found reference class forecasting superior to Monte Carlo and earned-value forecasting only under high similarity [f10070, f9606]. Schedule-risk analysis assigns task-duration ranges and risk events, then Monte Carlo simulation follows the dependency network thousands of times to estimate completion-date probabilities; single-date plans are optimistic where parallel paths converge because of merge bias [f16324, f16326, f16327, f9633]. Plans should report P50 and P80 dates and the probability of meeting the fixed deadline, supported by an auditable integrated schedule, range assumptions, critical path, buffers and an S-curve; these confidence figures must come from the program's own model and cannot be inferred from this research [f205, f10171, f9640]. The illustrative cadence calls for a schedule model as exit evidence from October–November 2026 scoping, but prototype-delivery slippage was not treated as a planned branch in the research and should be modeled explicitly with a signpost and hedge [f9652, f10376, f10377]. GAO treats schedule-risk analysis as best practice and NASA requires joint confidence levels, but evidence that NASA's requirement improves program outcomes was not found; the skeptic's review also demands cost and schedule evidence under pessimistic correlation results [f9628, f9630, f9631, f11155].
